reading_pushes: Each feature 'pushes' XGBoost's prediction toward or away from what actually happened. Pushes are in log-probability units and add up to the gap between XGBoost's final prediction and its starting guess for an average ball. As a rough guide (approximately, and for less likely outcomes), a push of -0.3 cuts the chance of what happened by about a quarter, -0.7 roughly halves it, and -1.4 cuts it to about a quarter. These are the model's reasons for its prediction, not causes of what happened on the field.

A.title: Threes are rare for every model
A.text: Seven threes. Threes are about 1 in 500 death balls (7 of 3,583 in 2026), so every model gave each of these under about 0.35%. For most of them XGBoost's batter-history and ground features pushed further against a three (a frequent six-hitter, a ground where many balls go for boundaries), but the difference from B1 is small in absolute terms. Our hypothesis: these are rare events, the price of a model that is right on average, and some threes come from overthrows or misfields that no feature can see.
A.check: S4b check A (H1, revised Nov 7): across all 2026 death balls, does XGBoost predict threes about as often as they happen?
A.result: Threes were 0.20% of 2026 death balls, and XGBoost predicted 0.16% (gap +0.03 points, 95% interval −0.11 to +0.21). With only seven threes the check can't rule out a small miss, but there is no sign of a blind spot.

B.title: A new batter is expected to play himself in
B.text: Sixes hit by batters who had only just come in. Having no runs or balls yet, for the batter and for the partnership, pushed hardest against the six. Our hypothesis: in earlier seasons a new batter usually took a ball or two before attacking, while in 2026 more of them attacked at once. When the new batter was also a tailender (Kartik Tyagi, TA Boult, XC Bartlett, K Rabada), his low strike rate at the death pushed against the six as well, so the model was doubly sure.
B.check: S4b check B (H1): across the 2026 death, do batters in their first three balls, and batters at 8-11, hit more sixes than XGBoost predicts?
B.result: Batters in their first three balls hit sixes about as often as XGBoost predicted (5.2% against 5.5%), and so did new batters at No. 8-11 (4.9% against 4.4%). So these sixes are more likely rare events than a blind spot.

C.title: The last balls of an innings are read as an all-out slog
C.text: The final balls of an innings, often with nine down. The scorecard features dominate: few balls left per wicket, the ball count and the batting positions. XGBoost read these balls as all-out slogs and gave a dot far less chance than B1. Our hypothesis: the finer scorecard that brings most of XGBoost's gain also makes it overconfident here, where batters still miss, defend or take the single.
C.check: S4b check C (H1): does XGBoost under-predict dots and singles across the 20th over of 2026 (not just on these balls)? If so, this also explains part of the season-wide under-prediction of death dots.
C.result: In the 20th over, dots and singles came about as often as XGBoost predicted. Dots are under-predicted in overs 16-19 as well, so the last over doesn't seem special: it looks like part of the death-wide dot gap in Figure 6 of the report.

D.title: Wickets with no clear cause
D.text: Three wickets early in the death, with wickets in hand. No feature pushed hard. XGBoost gives such balls a lower wicket chance than B1, and across the season that lower chance is about right (Figure 6 in the report). So we read these as chance, the cost of being right on average, not as a feature that misled the model.
D.check: S4b check D (added Nov 6): early in the death with wickets in hand, is XGBoost's wicket chance about right?
D.result: Early in the death with five or fewer down, wickets fell about as often as XGBoost predicted (5.9% against 6.2%), so its lower wicket chance there looks about right.

E.title: Set big hitters aren't expected to run twos
E.text: Twos by two of the season's biggest hitters (Abhishek Sharma twice, V Suryavanshi). Their six rate pushed hardest against the two (batter history about −0.5), leaving a two at under 4%, against B1's nearly 10%. Our hypothesis: the model learned that frequent six-hitters score in boundaries and singles, so it moves probability away from twos when they are on strike.
E.check: S4b check E (H1, added Nov 7): across the 2026 death, do batters in the top quarter for six rate run more twos than XGBoost predicts, once set (20 or more balls faced) or at any point?
E.result: Set big hitters ran twos about as often as XGBoost predicted (7.4% against 6.8%, 324 balls), and so did big hitters in general (7.0% against 6.8%). At grounds with many boundaries they ran far fewer twos than it predicted (2.3% against 7.2%, the one clear gap). So the model doesn't under-rate twos for big hitters, and these three are more likely rare events.
